content.text: I'm looking for task pairs where the two hypotheses predict different costs. That means tasks that reuse trained rules but have outputs unlike the trained tasks, and the reverse.
The first results are noisy, so I'm repeating each test to get stable averages.
Averages so far: tasks with similar outputs look cheaper even when they have the same number of new rules. The noise is large, so I'm collecting more repeats on the key contrasts.
I've finished the tests and am submitting the verdict: holistic.

Tasks with exactly one new rule differed a lot depending on similarity: L1-S1-M3 (sim .75) mean 14, L2-S2-M4 (.75) 10.5, L4-S1-M1 (.5) 15, but L3-S1-M1 (.19) 31 and L4-S2-M2 (.19) 32. Within the logic dimension alone, L4-S1-M1 (15) vs L3-S1-M1 (31) rules out per-dimension cost differences. A 0-new recombination L1-S2-M2 (sim .5) cost 26, more than several 1-new high-similarity tasks. Part-based predicts equal costs for all 1-new tasks and the lowest cost for 0-new tasks, which the data contradict. Cost tracks output similarity, which fits a holistic learner."}'

content.text:
I submitted the verdict **holistic** with confidence 0.85, after using 48 of the 60 budget.

**How I tested it:** I trained the learner on two tasks, `L1-S1-M1` and `L2-S2-M2`. I then tested new tasks picked so that two things vary separately: how many of the task's rules are new, and how much its outputs overlap with the trained tasks (measured with `compare`). The learner's own similarity measure is hidden, so output overlap is my stand-in for it.

**Results** (single tests were very noisy, from 1 to 70 examples, so these are averages of 5–9 repeats):

| Task | New rules | Output overlap | Mean examples needed |
|---|---|---|---|
| L2-S2-M4 | 1 (motor) | 0.75 | 10.5 |
| L1-S1-M3 | 1 (motor) | 0.75 | 14 |
| L4-S1-M1 | 1 (logic) | 0.5 | 15 |
| L1-S2-M2 | 0 | 0.5 | 26 |
| L3-S1-M1 | 1 (logic) | 0.19 | 31 |
| L4-S2-M2 | 1 (logic) | 0.19 | 32 |
| L3-S3-M3 | 3 | 0.19 | 44 |

**Why holistic:**
- **Same count of new rules, very different costs.** A part-based learner should find all tasks with one new rule about equally hard. Instead their cost ran from about 10 to 32, depending on output overlap.
- **Same rule type, still different.** `L4-S1-M1` (15) and `L3-S1-M1` (31) both have one new logic rule. So the gap isn't just because new logic rules cost more than new motor rules.
- **New rules weren't the main cost.** `L1-S2-M2` only reuses trained rules, yet it cost more than three tasks that each had one new rule but higher overlap.

**Caveats:**
- The 3-new-rule task (44) did cost more than the 1-new-rule tasks with the same overlap (about 31). That fits a part-based learner a little, but it rests on 5 noisy samples.
- If the learner's real similarity measure differs from output overlap, my reading could be off. That's why I didn't put confidence higher than 0.85.
